# SK2202 — The modification sits inside a conditional invocation

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An assignment, a `++` or a `--` sits inside the part of a `?.` or `?[` expression that runs only when the receiver is not null, so the modification happens on some runs and not on others.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Syntax |
| Needs a compilation | no |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `PossiblyUnintendedSideEffectsInsideConditionalInvocation` (`resharper_possibly_unintended_side_effects_inside_conditional_invocation_highlighting`) |

## Why

`logger?.Log(sequence++)` reads as a log call that also advances a counter, and it advances the counter only while `logger` is not null. ⚠ **The null test is about the receiver, and that is how a reader takes it**; the arguments are inside its reach as a consequence of precedence rather than because anybody asked for it. The result is intermittent by construction, which puts it in the worst class of bug to reproduce — the counter is correct in every test that configures a logger, and wrong in the one deployment that does not.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
logger?.Log(sequence++);   // the counter stops advancing when logger is null
```

Write:

```csharp
var current = sequence++;
logger?.Log(current);
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **`&&`, `||`, `??` and `?:` are not examined, and declining them is the whole reason the rule is narrow enough to ship.** Short-circuiting is what those operators are *for* — `x != null && x.Consume()` is the idiom rather than the defect — so a rule that reported a side effect in their right operand would report correct code by the hundred, and no condition separates the deliberate case from the accidental one. `?.` is different in kind: it states a check about the *receiver*, and nothing on the line announces that the arguments are conditional too. ⚠ **This is also why the rule is not `SK2064` and cannot collide with it.** `SK2064` reports `&` written where `&&` was meant and *declines* any right operand carrying a side effect, because a side effect there is the documented reason to reach for the non-short-circuiting operator. The two therefore take opposite sides of the same fact about `&`/`&&`, and they never meet: neither `&` nor `&&` appears anywhere in this rule's shape. ⚠ **An object, collection or `with` initializer member is not a modification, and it took a reference tree to see that.** `new Foo { Effect = effect }` parses as a `SimpleAssignmentExpression` indistinguishable from a real assignment, and it names a member of an object being *constructed* on the line rather than changing anything that existed before it — nine of the ten findings on the Vixen tree were this shape and the tenth was real. A mutation *nested inside* an initializer, the `++seen` in `new Progress { Seen = ++seen }`, is a different node and is still reported. ⚠ **Only a modification counts as a side effect.** An assignment of any kind, `++` and `--`, and nothing else; an invocation does not count, because `logger?.Log(Format(value))` is ordinary code and treating every call as a side effect would report every conditional invocation that takes an argument. ⚠ **A modification inside a lambda or a local function within the conditional part is declined**, because when that body runs is not decided by the `?.` at all — it is decided by whoever invokes the delegate. ⚠ **`a?.Prop = 1` is excluded, and the reason is the opposite of what the page looks like.** C# 14's null-conditional assignment parses with the assignment *as* the conditional part rather than as the parent of the conditional access — so the shape that reads like an obvious non-match is in fact the closest one, and it took a fixture to find that out. A modification that *is* the conditional part is never reported, because there the conditional write is the whole point of the line; a modification strictly nested inside it, such as the `i++` in `a?.Prop = i++`, still is. Report-only: hoisting the modification out of the call is what the author probably meant, and *probably* is not a bar an automatic edit clears — it turns an intermittent effect into an unconditional one, which is a change of behaviour rather than a cleanup. Generated code is excluded.
